title: Masculinity is Ours to Keep: Male Power Fantasy and Masculine Archetypes in Grappler Baki
summary: A scripted video essay using Grappler Baki to defend male power fantasies as the cultural vehicle of masculinity. NH argues masculinity rests on biology plus learned culture, that the West is deconstructing it, and that positive masculinity is born from confronting its negative side, as Baki does with his father Yujiro. He closes with a call to embody these values and become a role model.
claims: Masculinity is rooted in male hormones, which give men muscle, height, a square jaw, broad shoulders, a low voice and aggression
Masculinity works on two interconnected fronts, mental and physical, both stemming from biology
Male power fantasies show readers not who they are but who they wish to be, and they are the soil in which male identity grows
Much of masculinity is learned cultural standards passed down orally and through literature
Previous generations of men failed modern men, and Western media now works to deconstruct masculine values
A country's masculine traditions are its last line of defense, which is why masculinity is under constant attack
A generation raised without masculine role models will produce either aggressive, low self-control men or pacified, weak men
Only masculinity can oppose the violence that masculinity produces, so it must be kept 'in stock'
Anime and manga, especially Japanese shonen, are the most effective way to pass masculine values to younger men today
Values stick when shown through a hero's journey rather than told
Baki starts young and small at 13 so readers can identify with him and grow alongside him
Yujiro Hanma, Baki's father, represents paroxysmal masculinity that can only be measured against, and positive masculinity is born in response to it
Masculinity is built through confrontation, positive role models depend on negative ones, and masculine traits pass on cyclically through father-son antagonism
It is wrong to call toxic masculinity simply bad, since positive masculinity exists as a balancing response to it
Baki's fights work like the labors of Hercules, each victory symbolizing a win over the self
Critics who see only brutality in such stories are sheltered from violence by the masculine protection they condemn
As the world gets harsher, a man must become harsher or he won't be able to protect what is precious to him
In male power fantasies violence is never normalized; it is used to fight violence or to prepare for its inevitable arrival
Being weak isn't virtuous; a man who cannot defend himself loses his self-respect
Ancient masculinity wasn't toxic, it was whole; trying to keep only its nice parts destroys it
Being a man is about what you do, not only what you are: act on the blueprint and you become a power fantasy for others
